summary: No direct estimate exists for a 1912 vote without Roosevelt's party. Leads suggest Progressive voters would split, with many going to Wilson and Republicans in the Midwest staying with Taft. The 1924 La Follette run is an analogue with different coalitions. No numeric transfer estimates were found.

notes:
## Summary
The searches did not find direct evidence for your three questions. They found no scholarship that estimates a no-Roosevelt 1912 vote. They found nothing on how Midwestern and Western progressives voted in 1908. They found nothing on abstention when a progressive ticket was absent. They also found no breakdown by sex, nativity or race for 1912. Wikipedia-derived and Citizendium items below are leads only, not findings.

## 1. Direct evidence (1912 and 1910)
- **Counterfactual work:** An NBER working paper (2024) models what the Progressive candidacies changed. It argues that Roosevelt and other Progressive candidates shaped the 1912 outcome, including an unusually large Democratic House class. Roosevelt and other Progressive Party candidates clearly influenced the outcome of the 1912 election, and an unusually high number of Democrats won seats in the 63rd Congress. [S4] I did not retrieve its vote-transfer estimates.
- **Where Progressive voters would have gone:** A Citizendium entry, which is weak evidence, says at least half the nation's independent progressives went to Wilson's camp [S3]. It also says some Roosevelt opponents, such as La Follette, voted for Wilson rather than waste a vote on Taft [S3]. Treat both as unverified.
- **Democratic progressives stayed put:** An Ohio History Journal study finds that progressives in the Democratic Party remained united behind Wilson [S5]. It also finds that many Republican voters would back Roosevelt for the Republican nomination but would not take the next step and support [S5] the new party. That suggests many Republicans in Ohio, in the Midwest, would have stayed with the Republican ticket.
- **Taft's weakness:** Most of La Follette's supporters switched to Roosevelt. [S2] That implies the insurgent pool was already organised around a non-Taft candidate.
- **1910 midterms:** Republicans lost 57 House seats and Democrats took the House for the first time since 1894. [S1] James E. Campbell suggests one cause may have been many progressive voters choosing third-party candidates over conservative Republicans. [S1] This comes from Wikipedia, so check Campbell directly. It is the only evidence I found on behaviour before the new party existed. I found nothing on 1908.
- **Abstention:** I found no figures.

## 2. Analogues
- **1912 (the actual run):** Roosevelt drew 4.1 million votes (27%), behind Wilson's 42% and ahead of Taft's 23%, with Debs at 6%. [S2] This was the best third-party showing since the modern two-party system was established in 1864. [S2]
- **California, 1912:** Progressives took over the Republican Party and Taft was not even on the November ballot. [S2] This is the nearest case of an insurgent running inside a major-party line.
- **1924 (La Follette):** He won 4,827,184 votes (16.6%) and 13 electoral votes. [S19]
  - **Regions:** His strength lay in the East North Central and West North Central sections. [S10] He averaged 30% in the Pacific and Mountain states and 24% in the ten largest cities. [S15] In the former Confederacy he took 4.80%, against Coolidge's 27.94%. [S10]
  - **Groups:** One estimate is that about 52% of his support came from farmers, 20% from socialists, 20% from AFL union members and 8% from railroad workers. [S11] Some of his strongest support came from Germans and Scandinavians, and he did well in working-class Jewish and Italian districts of New York City. [S15]
  - **Black voters:** Although many prominent Black leaders endorsed him, most African Americans voted for their usual parties. [S15]
  - **Effect on the majors:** It cut into liberal Democratic voters [S10]. His inroads into the Republican vote came where Republicans could afford to be second or third [S10]. The sources I found do not give a Republican/Democratic split of his voters.
  - **Turnout:** Barely more than 50% of eligible voters took part in 1924. [S15]
- **Famous non-politician:** I found nothing on one in this period. I did not search for it.
- **Sex:** I found nothing on men versus women, and the scenario's "male" focus has no evidence behind it here.

## 3. Named people
- **Roosevelt:** When he was about seventy delegate votes short, he announced he was leaving the Republican Party and forming a new party. [S9] The Progressive convention then nominated Roosevelt and Hiram Johnson. [S2]
- **La Follette:** He was already challenging Taft [S2] before Roosevelt entered. I found nothing dated on his plans if Roosevelt had stayed out.
- **Johnson:** He was elected California governor in 1910 and stayed a Republican because his supporters controlled the party there. [S3]

## 4. Limits
- **Different parties:** 1924 was a farmer–labor, Socialist-backed coalition. By contrast, the Roosevelt party was middle and upper class [S14], so its voters do not map onto La Follette's.
- **Organisation:** The Progressives had little time to build the machinery to bring out voters. Progressive statewide candidates trailed Roosevelt's vote by about 20% [S3]. This suggests much of the vote followed Roosevelt personally and might not have followed a different progressive.
- **Missing data:** I found no Republican/Democratic split for either insurgent run. I found no abstention data. I found nothing by nativity or race for 1912, and nothing on enfranchised women in 1912 states.
- **Source quality:** Most of the 1912 material is secondary or encyclopaedic. The NBER paper, the Ohio study and Campbell are the leads worth pulling.
prompt:
Scenario for the 1912 United States presidential election (election day 1912-11-05).
A reader asked: "Theodore Roosevelt doesn't run as the Progressive candidate in 1912.".
As modelled: The former President's new party of progressive insurgents fields no presidential candidate, and the third candidate is off the ballot.
Kind of change: candidate. Populations it reaches first: sex: M.
Include the strongest third-party and independent runs nearest in time (1912 and 1924 above all), which groups they drew from and what share they took; and any run by a famous non-politician.

Questions to answer:
- Where Progressive voters in 1912 had previously voted, how did they split between the two major parties when no insurgent ticket was offered, as in comparable cases?
- How did progressive-leaning voters in the Midwest and West behave in 1908 and in the 1910 midterms, before the new party existed?
- In state elections where a progressive ticket was absent or a local insurgent withdrew, how many such voters abstained rather than choosing a major nominee?

Groups the simulation distinguishes: men and women; native-born white, naturalized immigrant, non-citizen immigrant and Black adults; the Northeast, Midwest, South (the eleven former Confederate states), border states and West. Evidence by these groups is most useful.
